one_sentence_story: When Harvard researchers asked volunteers to count basketball passes between players in white shirts, half of all viewers completely missed a person in a full gorilla suit who walked into the middle of the game and thumped her chest for nine seconds.
so_what_for_you: Looking right at something with open eyes does not guarantee you will see it: whenever your brain narrows its attention spotlight onto one task—like checking your phone or watching for cars at a crosswalk—it actively erases unexpected hazards standing directly in front of you.

jargon_map.plain: failing to see something in plain sight because your mind is busy with another task
jargon_map.analogy: Like searching a crowded room for a friend in a red coat and looking straight through another friend waving at you in a blue coat.

jargon_map.plain: vision center at the back of your brain
jargon_map.analogy: Like a camera sensor that receives every ray of light from the room before the editor decides what makes the final cut.
Like a stage spotlight operator who illuminates the actors in white shirts and leaves everyone in dark clothing in the shadows.

jargon_map.plain: hunting for one specific colour or target while blocking everything else
jargon_map.analogy: Like setting a spam filter that only lets messages with the word 'white' into your inbox and silently deletes the rest.

jargon_map.plain: pointing the sharp center of your eyes directly at an object
jargon_map.analogy: Aiming a flashlight straight at a gorilla's chest while your mind is too busy counting to notice what is in the beam.
